newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish bid for early election faces problems.
newsitem.headline: Turkish bid for early election faces problems.

text.p: Turkey's first Islamist leader, Necmettin Erbakan, is betting he can renew his battered mandate with early elections, but analysts say he may face problems placing his fate in the hands of the people.
Commentators point to major institutional and political hurdles standing in the way of the government's bid to stage snap elections.
Prime Minister Erbakan told a news conference on Sunday his government, its absolute majority in parliament now a thing of the past, had resolved to seek an early vote for the good of the country.
"We decided that for Turkey to continue its economic success, an early election would be necessary," said Erbakan, flanked by his secularist coalition partner Tansu Ciller.
"We believe we (the coalition partners) will come back stronger if we go to elections."
No date was announced, but both leaders said they would seek to stage the elections as soon as possible. Polls were normally due by the year 2000.
Under Turkish law parliament must set the date for elections -- a challenge for a coalition which has seen its absolute parliamentary majority bleed away in recent days.
MPs would also have to approve the coalition's announced plans to make Ciller prime minister in a caretaker "election government".
The inability to pass an election law might give the secularist opposition an opening to form a new government.
President Suleyman Demirel could nominate an opposition figure to try to set up a new administration if the coalition did not get support for snap polls.
"There are serious obstacled to any early polls," political commentator Bilal Cetin told Reuters.
"Parliament is only two years old so it would be very difficult to get approval for new elections," Cetin said.
Analysts say opposition can be expected from wary government MPs -- particularly in Ciller's ill-disciplined True Path Party. Many are fearful of risking the substantial privileges of office.
Others worry Ciller may not reappoint them to party lists once an election is set in motion.
"It certainly looks like a roll of the dice," said one Western diplomat. "I think the risk of failure for Erbakan is greater inside parliament than it is with the people," the diplomat said.

The Welfare Party's Erbakan exploited deep divisons among the secularist parties to become modern Turkey's first Islamist leader after winning a slim plurality of 21 percent in the last general elections, held in December 1995.

He teamed up with secularist Ciller -- who had earlier denounced the Islam-based Welfare as representing the "forces of darkness" -- after promising to drop corruption charges the party had filed against her.
However, their partnership soon soured as Welfare partisans began to demand a greater role for Islam in the public life of officially secular Turkey.

The powerful armed forces, spearheading a secularist counterattack, in February demanded Erbakan's government stem what it saw as the rising tide of Islamist activism. It has stepped up the warnings ever since.
Pressure from the traditional elite, in particular from the respected army commanders, touched off a series of defections from Ciller's True Path wing of the government.

The resignation of a senior conservative MP on Friday left the government clinging to just 275 seats in the 550-member parliament, one short of the majority needed to win a confidence vote. Two seats are vacant.
A combative Ciller appeared unbowed by the prospects, challenging the opposition to try its luck in fresh polls.
"Let's ask, let the people decide," she told the joint news conference with Erbakan. "It's interesting that when we say 'the people', when we say 'democracy', the opposition disappears."
